title: How close is Russia to unplugging from the internet?
text: EUvsDisinfo – analiza: How close is Russia to unplugging from the internet?. Will Russia attempt to isolate itself from the world wide web and replace it by a domestic internet? Controversial discussions between two Russian ministries indicate that the option is at least on the table. As we underlined in December , Russia's new “Information security doctrine” suggests that the Kremlin's long term goal is to have its right to control Russia's information space accepted internationally on a par with a state's right to have its territorial integrity respected. Along this line, the doctrine includes a vague formulation about “the development of a national system to control the Russian segment of the internet”. An understanding of how this passage in the doctrine will be implemented has now surfaced as the result of public controversies between the Russian Ministry of Communications and the Ministry of Economic Development. As reported by Vedomosti , Russia's Communications Ministry has drafted a law on “a sovereign internet” to regulate internet traffic so that the country, if it finds itself under a large-scale cyber attack, can unplug from the internet. The problem is that in order to make this technically possible, internet providers will be forced to direct all communications through specific traffic exchange points inside Russia, instead of being free to choose the fastest and thereby least costly connections. The traditionally more business-friendly Ministry of Economic Development has listened to the Russian internet providers and now warns that the law could make the price of internet access in Russia soar. Leaving the cost issue aside, there are fears that the doctrine's "national system to control the Russian segment of the internet” will not only be a defensive contingency measure in case of sudden and massive hostile cyber attacks from abroad, but that Russia will try to unplug from the internet when it could be politically convenient. In a society where the government systematically marginalises independent media and where a “foreign agents law” isolates civil society organisations from the surrounding world, moves towards also de-globalising the Russian internet would not come as a great surprise. Interviewed in a RFE/RL radio show this Sunday , Irina Borogan and Andrei Soldatov, authors of The Red Web , said that Russia is indeed aiming at a “Chinese solution” of limiting internet freedom.
